newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian PM urges farmers to halt milk protest.
newsitem.headline: Italian PM urges farmers to halt milk protest.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi urged farmers on Sunday to halt protests over European Union milk quotas which have brought chaos to Italy's financial capital for four days.
Farmers descended on Milan with hundreds of tractors and set up road blocks around the main airport, Linate, forcing passengers to walk for kilometres (miles) to catch their planes.

Blockades also created problems for fans trying to get to Milan's San Siro stadium for Sunday's Serie A clash between Internazionale and Bologna, while the farmers threatened to extend their action to the city's second airport, Malpensa.
Prodi told reporters that he was prepared to listen to the farmers' grievances if they cleared the roads first.
"I'm ready to meet the farmers in Rome so long as they halt this illegal action," he said, adding that his government had been working with Brussels for weeks to try to resolve the problems.
The European Union slapped 370 billion lire ($235 million) of fines on Italian dairy farmers for exceeding their milk quotas in the 1995-96 season.
Farmers have called on the state to pay the levies and say a draft law aimed at compensating them for the fines does not go far enough. They also say the EU quotas must be raised.

The government has offered cheap-rate loans to the farmers but refused to take responsibility for the fines. "The Italian government is firmly committed to giving relief to farmers, but it cannot disobey European Union rules," Prodi said.
Farmers earlier warned that they could keep up their protests until late March, when they have to return to the land to sow crops. Police have so far made no attempt to move the protesters.

"Farmers are ready to come from all over the north of Italy to demonstrate," said Alberto Oldani, a farm labourer at the San Siro blockade. "Yesterday we shut down one area of the city, today two, tomorrow five or six."

The farmers' unofficial leader Aldo Bettinelli said they had fallen foul of tough EU quotas, introduced in the 1980s, which allowed them to produce under 60 percent of Italy's milk needs. The rest is imported from other EU countries.
"The state made the mistake, they have to pay for it," Bettinelli told La Stampa newspaper. "Day after day this protest will grow."
An airport official warned that it would shortly run out of aircraft fuel unless the Linate blockade was lifted.

Italian Agriculture Minister Michele Pinto is due to go to Brussels on Monday and is expected to seek concessions from the European Commission. The Commission has already lowered the original fine from 421 billion lire to 370 billion.
"We have now reached the moment when these fines can no longer not be paid," Prodi said.
Fearing that the protests might spread to the capital, Rome's prefect (regional governor) banned the use of all agricultural vehicles on roads within a five km (three miles) radius of the city.
